prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN) -- The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is working with public health officials in 42 states to determine the cause of an outbreak of a particular type of salmonella called Typhimurium. Salmonella bacteria are transmitted to humans by eating contaminated foods. According to CDC sources, at least 388 people have been infected with this strain since September 3, but most cases occurred between October 1 and December 31, the disease agency said. About 18 percent of cases were hospitalized as a result of their illness, and patients have ranged from two months to 98 years of age. California is reporting the highest case count with 55, followed by Ohio with 53 cases, Massachusetts with 39, Minnesota with 30 and Michigan with 20. The other 37 states are each reporting anywhere from one to 19 cases. The eight states that have not reported any cases connected to the outbreak are Montana, New Mexico, Louisiana, Mississippi, South Carolina, Florida, Alaska and Hawaii. King Nut peanut butter was identified as the source of an outbreak that may have contributed to one death in Minnesota, state public health officials said Friday in a news release. CNN was unable to reach the company for comment. CDC has not identified what food or foods might be causing this outbreak. CDC officials and state public health workers are conducting case control studies, which means they're tracking down people who have been infected as early as September to determine what they may have consumed, to find a common cause.  Learn more about salmonella » . The Food and Drug Administration and the U.S. Department of Agriculture are in contact with the CDC, but without a determination of the cause of the outbreak, their involvement is limited. Various strains of salmonella have been linked to previous outbreaks, caused by contaminated eggs, meat, poultry, vegetables, pet food and even peanut butter. Contaminated tomatoes were blamed for a salmonella Typhimurium outbreak in fall 2006, which sickened at least 183 people in 21 states. Most of the victims had diarrhea and fever for about a week. Nobody died in that outbreak. Salmonella infections are caused by bacteria and if necessary can be treated with antibiotics, although some strains have become resistant to these drugs, according to the CDC Web site. Most people infected will develop diarrhea, fever and abdominal cramps within a few days of infection, and their illness can last up to a week. Most recover without any treatment, but some may suffer dehydration and in severe cases require hospitalization. The youngest and oldest patients and chronically ill people with compromised immune systems are at highest risk for severe complications, according to the National Institutes of Health. Until a cause of the outbreak is confirmed, the CDC is recommending the following: . Consumers should thoroughly cook meats, poultry and eggs. They should also avoid consuming raw or unpasteurized milk and other dairy products. Produce should be thoroughly washed as well. Avoid cross-contamination of uncooked meats and produce to prevent spreading any potential salmonella. Frequent washing of hands during food preparation can also help reduce cross-contamination.

CDC sources said at least 388 people had been infected with this strain since September 3, with most illnesses occurring from October 1 through December 31. Patients ranged in age from two months to 98 years, and approximately 18 percent required hospitalization.

Federal and state health investigators were carrying out case-control studies, tracing people infected as far back as September and examining what they had eaten in hopes of identifying a shared source.

The Food and Drug Administration and the U.S. Department of Agriculture were communicating with the CDC, but their roles remained limited because the outbreak’s cause had not yet been established.

Previous salmonella outbreaks involving various strains have been associated with contaminated eggs, meat, poultry, vegetables, pet food and even peanut butter. Most patients recover without medical treatment. Some, however, can become dehydrated, and severe cases may require hospitalization. To limit possible salmonella transmission, people should keep uncooked meat separate from produce and wash their hands frequently while preparing food.

**CDC investigates multistate salmonella outbreak linked to peanut butter**

**ATLANTA** — The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is investigating a multistate outbreak of *Salmonella Typhimurium* that has sickened at least 388 people across 42 states.

Federal and state health officials say epidemiological evidence suggests peanut butter — including peanut butter used in some commercially prepared foods — may be a source of the infections. Investigators are working to identify the products involved and determine how widely they were distributed.

Salmonella symptoms typically include diarrhea, fever and abdominal cramps beginning 12 to 72 hours after exposure. Illness usually lasts four to seven days, and most people recover without treatment. Severe infections can occur, however, particularly among young children, older adults and people with weakened immune systems.

Consumers are advised to check CDC and US Food and Drug Administration recall notices before eating peanut butter or peanut butter-containing products. Recalled items should be discarded or returned to the place of purchase.

Health officials also recommend washing hands with soap and water before preparing food and after handling potentially contaminated products, cleaning kitchen surfaces and utensils, and avoiding cross-contamination. Anyone experiencing severe diarrhea, persistent fever, dehydration or other serious symptoms should contact a health care provider.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed news article on the 2008–2009 U.S. salmonella outbreak, mentioning state case counts, hospitalization rates, the King Nut peanut butter connection, and the ongoing CDC investigation.
counterfactuals.output:
# Salmonella Outbreak Spread Across 46 States as Investigators Traced Illnesses to Peanut Products

**ATLANTA —** A nationwide salmonella outbreak that began in 2008 sickened at least 714 people in 46 states and was ultimately linked to peanut butter and peanut paste produced at a Georgia processing plant, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

The outbreak, caused by *Salmonella enterica* serotype Typhimurium, led to 166 reported hospitalizations—about 23% of known patients—and was associated with nine deaths. Illnesses began as early as September 2008 and continued into 2009, while federal and state agencies conducted an extensive investigation and companies recalled thousands of foods containing peanut ingredients.

Ohio reported the largest number of cases, with 102, followed by California with 81. Other heavily affected states included New York with 50 cases, Massachusetts with 49, Minnesota with 44 and Michigan with 38. Cases were also reported across the South, Midwest, Northeast and West, demonstrating the broad reach of the contaminated products. Because many people with salmonellosis do not seek medical care or undergo laboratory testing, investigators cautioned that the true number of illnesses was likely substantially higher.

## King Nut peanut butter provided an early break

A key development came when Minnesota health officials identified the outbreak strain of salmonella in an open, five-pound container of King Nut brand creamy peanut butter. The product had been collected from a long-term-care facility where residents had become ill.

King Nut, an Ohio-based distributor, did not manufacture the peanut butter. The product was made by Peanut Corporation of America, or PCA, at its plant in Blakely, Georgia, and sold under the King Nut and Parnell’s Pride labels. The large containers were distributed primarily to institutions, including nursing homes, hospitals, schools, restaurants and food-service operations, rather than through ordinary supermarket retail channels.

King Nut issued a recall in January 2009 after being told that the outbreak strain had been detected in the product. The finding helped investigators focus on the Georgia facility and the peanut ingredients it supplied to other manufacturers.

The inquiry soon expanded beyond jars of institutional peanut butter. PCA also produced peanut paste and other ingredients used in cookies, crackers, snack bars, candy, ice cream, pet treats and additional processed foods. As federal investigators traced those ingredients through the supply chain, hundreds of companies announced recalls, eventually making the episode one of the largest food recalls in U.S. history.

## Investigation relied on laboratory matching and product tracing

The CDC worked with the Food and Drug Administration, state health departments and local public-health agencies to identify patients, compare food histories and match bacterial samples through PulseNet, the national network that uses DNA fingerprinting to detect outbreaks.

Patients were questioned about foods they had eaten and the institutions or facilities where they had been served. Investigators then traced suspected products back through distributors and manufacturers. Laboratory tests of food and environmental samples helped connect illnesses in widely separated states to a common source.

The FDA’s inspection of the Blakely plant found serious sanitation and production concerns. Federal officials said the investigation covered not only the original King Nut product but also the broader distribution of PCA’s peanut butter and peanut paste.

## Severe illness among vulnerable patients

Salmonella infection commonly causes diarrhea, fever and abdominal cramps, usually beginning 12 to 72 hours after exposure. Most people recover without treatment in four to seven days, but the infection can become severe when the bacteria spread from the intestines into the bloodstream.

Infants, older adults and people with weakened immune systems face a higher risk of hospitalization or death. The outbreak’s connection to institutional food service was particularly concerning because some contaminated peanut butter had been served in nursing homes and other facilities housing medically vulnerable residents.

The roughly 23% hospitalization rate underscored the seriousness of the outbreak. Officials noted, however, that some reported deaths occurred in patients with other significant medical conditions, and public-health authorities reviewed each case to determine the role of salmonella.

## CDC inquiry continued as recalls widened

During the height of the outbreak, the CDC described the investigation as ongoing, with new illnesses, laboratory results and product-distribution records still being evaluated. Case totals changed as states submitted reports and investigators determined whether each infection matched the outbreak strain.

Officials advised consumers to check FDA recall lists rather than assume that all peanut butter was unsafe. Major national brands of retail jarred peanut butter were not broadly implicated; the principal concern was PCA-made peanut butter and peanut paste and the many foods manufactured with those ingredients.

The final reported total reached 714 cases in 46 states, but health authorities emphasized that confirmed cases represented only a portion of the people likely sickened. The King Nut finding proved to be the crucial early link, turning a geographically scattered cluster of infections into a focused investigation of a single processor and a complex national supply chain.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain the nationwide salmonella investigation, covering the CDC’s case-control studies, the possible Minnesota death, prior outbreaks, common symptoms and treatments, vulnerable populations, and recommended food-handling precautions.
counterfactuals.output:
The nationwide investigation was an effort by the CDC, FDA, and state health departments to determine whether salmonellosis cases reported in many states came from a common food source.

### CDC case-control studies
Investigators used case-control studies: they interviewed people with laboratory-confirmed Salmonella infection and compared their recent food purchases, meals, travel, and other exposures with those of similar people who remained healthy. Foods reported significantly more often by patients became leads, but an association alone did not prove contamination. Investigators also examined restaurant clusters, grocery records, product distribution chains, and laboratory “fingerprints” of the bacteria. Early studies can implicate one food while later work identifies another ingredient or point in the supply chain.

### Possible Minnesota death
Minnesota reported a death involving a person infected with the outbreak strain, but officials initially treated it as *possibly associated*, not necessarily caused by salmonellosis. That distinction matters because patients—particularly older adults or those with serious underlying illnesses—may die while infected even when another condition is the principal cause.

### Previous outbreaks
Salmonella outbreaks have repeatedly been linked to eggs, poultry, meat, raw produce, sprouts, melons, tomatoes or peppers, nut products, and processed foods. Infections have also come from reptiles, amphibians, backyard poultry, and contaminated pet food. Earlier outbreaks showed that contamination can occur on farms, during processing or packing, in restaurants, or in home kitchens, and that apparently dry or intact foods are not automatically safe.

### Symptoms and treatment
Symptoms generally begin **6 hours to 6 days after exposure** and commonly include:

- Diarrhea, sometimes severe or bloody  
- Fever  
- Abdominal cramps  
- Nausea or vomiting  
- Headache and fatigue  

Most people recover in about **four to seven days** with rest and fluids. Oral rehydration is the main treatment; severe dehydration may require intravenous fluids. Antibiotics are usually reserved for severe or invasive infection and for patients at high risk of complications, because routine antibiotic use may not shorten ordinary intestinal illness. Antidiarrheal medicines should be used only after medical advice, especially when fever or bloody diarrhea is present.

Seek medical care for bloody diarrhea, persistent high fever, signs of dehydration, symptoms lasting more than a few days, or illness in a high-risk person.

### People at greater risk
Severe infection is more likely in:

- Infants and young children  
- Adults 65 and older  
- Pregnant people  
- People with weakened immune systems  
- People with serious chronic illnesses  

In these groups, Salmonella can enter the bloodstream and cause life-threatening infection elsewhere in the body.

### Food-handling precautions
Authorities generally recommend:

- Follow outbreak-specific recalls and do not eat suspected products; discard or return them as instructed.  
- Wash hands with soap before preparing food and after handling raw meat, eggs, animals, pet food, or using the bathroom.  
- Keep raw meat, poultry, seafood, and eggs separate from ready-to-eat foods.  
- Use separate cutting boards and utensils, and wash surfaces with hot, soapy water.  
- Cook foods to safe internal temperatures and refrigerate perishables within two hours—one hour in very hot conditions.  
- Avoid raw or undercooked eggs, poultry, meat, and unpasteurized milk or juice.  
- Rinse produce under running water, while recognizing that washing cannot reliably remove contamination that has entered the food.  
- Do not wash raw poultry, because splashing can spread bacteria around the kitchen.  
- High-risk people should be especially cautious with raw sprouts, undercooked eggs and meat, and unpasteurized products.  

Anyone who is ill should avoid preparing food for others and practice meticulous hand hygiene, since Salmonella may continue to be shed after symptoms improve.
